title: Germ theory of disease
summary: Throughout the early 1860s Louis Pasteur ran experiments to prove his atmospheric germ theory, which held that microorganisms travel through the air, and his work opposed spontaneous generation. Later in the century, techniques introduced by Pasteur, Robert Koch and others led to the discovery of a myriad of bacteria. Pasteur's studies popularized the germ theory of disease and raised hope that vaccination could prevent infectious diseases.

uncertainty.note: Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation and established atmospheric germs in the early 1860s; Robert Koch subsequently isolated specific bacterial pathogens between 1876 and 1882.

as_recorded.value: Throughout the early 1860s, Pasteur conducted a series of experiments
popularized the germ theory of disease

when.display: from the 1860s to the late 19th century

importance.justification: Germ theory transformed medicine by identifying microscopic pathogens as the cause of infectious diseases, enabling antiseptic surgery, vaccines, and modern sanitation.

related.because: Early observations of clinical contagion in obstetrics foreshadowed microbial transmission before germ theory was accepted.

reviewer_note: Others, including Semmelweis, Lister and Koch, were also involved. The end date is approximate, since the sources say only the latter half of the century. The pin at Paris is a stand-in.
